microGPT in Fortress: a transformer written as mathematics

A complete GPT — tokenizer, autograd, model, loss, Adam, sampling — expressed in Sun Labs' Fortress language so that its executable definitions typeset as the formulas of the papers, verified against Andrej Karpathy's microgpt to machine precision. The article teaches two things side by side: how a GPT works, and how to build the Fortress building blocks that let its mathematical core be written so directly.

What you are looking at. Every Fortress figure below is typeset by Fortify, the project's own Emacs-and-LaTeX typesetter, from the exact ASCII source that the Fortress interpreter runs (open “ASCII source as typed” under any figure). Nothing is hand-typeset. The behavioral reference is the pinned microgpt.py gist (revision 14fb0388…, sha256 d47d88c2…); the Fortress program reproduces its logits, losses, all 4192 gradients, the Adam-updated parameters and its sampled names for two training steps and three samples with maximum differences at the level of floating-point rounding (≤ 3·10-16). Section 7 has the numbers.

1. How to read the figures

Fortress (Sun Labs, 2003–2012) was designed so that programs read like whiteboard mathematics: Unicode or ASCII-spelled operators, juxtaposition as a user-definable multiplication, big operators such as SUM defined in libraries, and a typesetter that turns the ASCII you type into the notation you mean. The four lines below are a running Fortress program; on the left is what Fortify makes of them.

Conventions to keep in mind: SUM[x_i <- x] x_i^2 is a real reduction over the elements of x (typeset ∑ with its binding below); <| e | x <- g |> is a list comprehension (⟨ e | x ← g ⟩); x DOT w is the operator named DOT (·); identifiers such as alpha or x_i are typeset as α and xi; a name in [\ … \] is a static (type or size) argument and typesets in white brackets ⟦…⟧; keywords are in typewriter. Fortress code is implicitly parallel: the iterations of a comprehension or a reduction may run in separate threads, and the language keeps that order-independence visible rather than hiding it.

Three colors of code appear in this article. Python excerpts (blue) are quoted verbatim from the pinned reference. Fortress figures (cards) are typeset from the actual program. Plain grey blocks are interpreter output or shell commands.

2. Autograd: a scalar that remembers the chain rule

Training needs, for every parameter, the derivative of the loss with respect to it. microgpt gets it by reverse-mode automatic differentiation on scalars: every number in the computation is wrapped in a Value that records which values it was computed from and the local derivative with respect to each. Backpropagation then walks the graph from the loss backwards, applying the chain rule at each node:

The local derivatives of the six operations microgpt uses are:

Here is the reference class, minus the reverse-operand helpers:

class Value:
    def __init__(self, data, children=(), local_grads=()):
        self.data = data                # scalar value of this node calculated during forward pass
        self.grad = 0                   # derivative of the loss w.r.t. this node, calculated in backward pass
        self._children = children       # children of this node in the computation graph
        self._local_grads = local_grads # local derivative of this node w.r.t. its children

    def __add__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        return Value(self.data + other.data, (self, other), (1, 1))

    def __mul__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        return Value(self.data * other.data, (self, other), (other.data, self.data))

    def __pow__(self, other): return Value(self.data**other, (self,), (other * self.data**(other-1),))
    def log(self): return Value(math.log(self.data), (self,), (1/self.data,))
    def exp(self): return Value(math.exp(self.data), (self,), (math.exp(self.data),))
    def relu(self): return Value(max(0, self.data), (self,), (float(self.data > 0),))

The Fortress version is an object whose operator methods define +, juxtaposition (Fortress's multiplication: a b means a·b), ^, and the functions log, exp, relu. Each result is built by node(data, (child, ∂/∂child) …): the dependencies are pairs of a child and the local derivative with respect to it, which is exactly the information the chain rule consumes. The pairs are a variable-length argument list (deps: (Value, RR64)...) of a small factory function, because Fortress objects cannot declare varargs constructors.

Read opr +(self, b: Value): Value = node(data + b.data, (self, 1), (b, 1)) against the first two local derivatives above: the sum's value is data + b.data, and its derivative is 1 with respect to each operand. Multiplication records (self, b.data) and (b, data); the power records n·datan−1; log records 1/data. Python's __radd__/__rmul__/__truediv__ helpers become overloads that accept a plain RR64 on either side; −a, a − b and a / b are derived exactly as in the reference (a·(−1), a + (−b), a·b−1), so the two programs build the same graph.

The backward method is the chain rule verbatim: set ∂L/∂L = 1, visit the nodes in reverse topological order, and for each dependency (c, d) of a node v accumulate c.grad += d · v.grad. Compare with the reference:

    def backward(self):
        topo = []
        visited = set()
        def build_topo(v):
            if v not in visited:
                visited.add(v)
                for child in v._children:
                    build_topo(child)
                topo.append(v)
        build_topo(self)
        self.grad = 1
        for v in reversed(topo):
            for child, local_grad in zip(v._children, v._local_grads):
                child.grad += local_grad * v.grad

The topological sort is the one piece of supporting machinery here. Python keys its visited set by object identity; Fortress's library Set is an ordered set, so every Value gets an integer id from an atomic counter (nextId()), which is what the local function visit records.

These 40 lines are the whole autograd engine. A first sanity check, taken from the microgpt article (L = a·b + a with a = 2, b = 3 gives ∂L/∂a = 4, ∂L/∂b = 2) and a finite-difference check on exp(ab) + ln b − a²/b agree with the Fortress gradients to 3·10-10 (the central-difference error; probes/probe11_backward.fss).

Two other shapes for the same node

Before settling on pairs, two other representations were built and run. The Python shape — two parallel lists, children and local gradients — works, but Fortress list literals infer the element type from the literals (<|1, 1|> is a list of integer literals, not of RR64), so every literal needs a static-argument annotation, and the backward pass needs an explicit zip:

The original micrograd shape — each node owns a closure that pushes its gradient to its children — also works, and is the most “object-oriented”, but the derivative is buried in imperative code and a function-valued field must be called as (v.propagate)():

The pairs form was chosen because it makes the two ingredients of the chain rule — which child and what local derivative — the literal arguments of every operation, and because it typesets without noise.

3. Summation, and how a user type joins the ∑ big operator

Everything else in a transformer is sums of products. Python writes sum(wi * xi for wi, xi in zip(wo, x)); the mathematics writes a ∑ with its index below. Fortress has ∑ as a big operator: SUM[i <- g] e (typeset ∑i←g e) desugars into a call of the generator's generate method with a reduction object — an associative join and an identity empty. The library defines that reduction for numbers only (opr SUM[\T extends Number\]()), and the Number trait is sealed (comprises { RR64 }), so a user type such as Value cannot simply become a Number.

What the language does provide is (a) the reduction protocol as ordinary library code, and (b) an except clause on the implicit import of the standard library. Hiding the library's nullary ∑ and defining a CommutativeMonoidReduction over Value makes ∑ available to autograd scalars with exactly the semantics of the mathematics — a monoid with identity 0 — while the library's ∑ over plain numbers is no longer visible in this component (the model never needs it):

import FortressLibrary.{...} except { opr BIG + }

Two details are worth knowing. The nullary form opr SUM() is what SUM[gs] body desugars to (the interpreter names the accumulator BIG + internally, hence the except spelling); the prefix form opr SUM(g) serves SUM xs on a whole list. And the identity element is node(0): like Python's built-in sum, which starts from the integer 0 and wraps it in a Value, a summation may add a zero leaf to the graph; it changes nothing numerically and the gradient flows through it correctly. Where the reference sums sequentially (a left fold), a Fortress reduction combines terms in whatever order the generator chooses — the differences this produces are the rounding-level discrepancies reported in section 7, and they are the price of not suppressing the language's parallelism.

A second question the exploration answered: could one ∑ serve scalars and vectors, as it does on paper (yt = ∑s αts vs)? A reduction over an Additive trait with an explicit Zero runs correctly for both in the interpreter, but the static type of such a sum is Additive, not Value or Vec: it works dynamically but a type checker would demand a cast, so it is shown as an alternative in section 9, not used.

4. Vectors and matrices of differentiable scalars

microgpt keeps vectors as Python lists of Values and matrices as lists of rows, and writes the three linear-algebra operations it needs as comprehensions:

def linear(x, w):
    return [sum(wi * xi for wi, xi in zip(wo, x)) for wo in w]
# ... inside gpt():
x = [t + p for t, p in zip(tok_emb, pos_emb)]
attn_logits = [sum(q_h[j] * k_h[t][j] for j in range(head_dim)) / head_dim**0.5 for t in range(len(k_h))]
head_out = [sum(attn_weights[t] * v_h[t][j] for t in range(len(v_h))) for j in range(head_dim)]

The mathematics names these: a dot product, a matrix–vector product taken row by row, and a row-vector–matrix product.

Fortress lets us give those names executable meaning. A Vec is a list of Values wrapped in an object so that operators can be attached to it; a Mat is a list of row Vecs. The wrapper costs six one-line delegations — bounds, indices, index/value pairs, size, subscript, slice — after which the library's DelegatedIndexed trait supplies everything a generator needs, so a Vec works inside comprehensions and under ∑ exactly like a list. The operators are then one line each: x + y, the dot product x DOT y (typeset ·), division by a scalar, concatenation x || y, scalar times vector by juxtaposition, and relu applied elementwise.

The last three lines define a second big operator: BIG || is the “concatenate all” version of ||, a monoid whose identity is the empty vector. It will join the attention heads.

A matrix subscripts as W[i] (a row), W[i, j] (an entry) and W[r] with a range (a block of rows); W.cols(r) selects columns. W.entries flattens the parameters for the optimizer. Juxtaposition is overloaded twice: W x is the matrix–vector product (each row dotted with x), and a M is the row-vector–matrix product ∑t at Mtj — the form in which attention weights multiply the cached values.

With these definitions the transformer below is written in the vocabulary of the formulas: W_q x, K q, alpha V, x + y, W_out relu(W_in x). The dot product of a row with x is a ∑ over Values, so every scalar multiply-add still becomes one node in the autograd graph, exactly as in the reference — the operators add notation, not a different computation.

Why wrappers, and not the library's own vectors

Fortress's specification abbreviates array types as T[n] and vector/matrix types as T^n, T^(m TIMES n), which typeset as the ℝn, ℝm×n of the papers. The sheet below (an exploration, not a running program) shows the candidate spellings side by side:

Only the first two rows of “type spellings” execute in this interpreter, and only with literal sizes: Value[n] with a nat parameter does not unify with the runtime array (an implementation gap), and Value^n parses but denotes the library's Vector, which is restricted to Number (a library gap). The verified first design of this experiment (src/alt/v1_MicroGPT.fss) used explicit Array2⟦Value,0,m,0,n⟧ weights and the index form of the product; it reads as textbook algebra but every signature carries the type noise:

The Vec/Mat pair trades twenty lines of user-level definitions for signatures such as rmsnorm(x: Vec): Vec and for attention written as softmax(K q/√d) V. Section 9 keeps the comparison.

5. The model

microgpt follows GPT-2 with three simplifications: RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm, no biases, ReLU instead of GeLU. Its gpt function processes one token at a time and keeps the keys and values of earlier positions in a cache. This article's primary form processes the whole sequence at once, which is how the papers write it; section 5.6 shows the one-token-at-a-time form, which is verified too.

5.1 RMSNorm

def rmsnorm(x):
    ms = sum(xi * xi for xi in x) / len(x)
    scale = (ms + 1e-5) ** -0.5
    return [xi * scale for xi in x]

The mean square is a ∑ over the elements of x divided by |x|; scale x is scalar–vector juxtaposition. The −0.5 power is the same node the Python builds (** -0.5).

5.2 Softmax

def softmax(logits):
    max_val = max(val.data for val in logits)
    exps = [(val - max_val).exp() for val in logits]
    total = sum(exps)
    return [e / total for e in exps]

BIG MAX is the library's maximum big operator over plain numbers (the shift m is a constant, not part of the graph, in both programs). Subtracting m before exponentiating is the standard overflow guard and does not change the result.

5.3 Attention

For each layer, every position's vector is projected to a query, a key and a value; a position attends to all positions up to itself: its query is scored against those keys, the scores become weights through softmax, and the weights mix the corresponding values. The reference does this one token at a time (the cached keys and values are the earlier positions'):

q = linear(x, state_dict[f'layer{li}.attn_wq'])
k = linear(x, state_dict[f'layer{li}.attn_wk'])
v = linear(x, state_dict[f'layer{li}.attn_wv'])
keys[li].append(k)
values[li].append(v)
x_attn = []
for h in range(n_head):
    hs = h * head_dim
    q_h = q[hs:hs+head_dim]
    k_h = [ki[hs:hs+head_dim] for ki in keys[li]]
    v_h = [vi[hs:hs+head_dim] for vi in values[li]]
    attn_logits = [sum(q_h[j] * k_h[t][j] for j in range(head_dim)) / head_dim**0.5 for t in range(len(k_h))]
    attn_weights = softmax(attn_logits)
    head_out = [sum(attn_weights[t] * v_h[t][j] for t in range(len(v_h))) for j in range(head_dim)]
    x_attn.extend(head_out)
x = linear(x_attn, state_dict[f'layer{li}.attn_wo'])

Written for the whole sequence X (one row per position) and one head h of width dh:

The Fortress layer is that formula. Q, K, V are matrices whose rows are W_q x, W_k x, W_v x for each position; .cols(c) restricts them to head h's columns; for position t, Kh[0:t] Qh[t] is the vector of scores against the keys of positions 0…t, and alpha Vh[0:t] is the row-vector–matrix product that mixes the values. The heads are concatenated with the BIG || operator and projected by W_o. Because every position is computed by a comprehension over X.indices, positions are independent iterations — in Fortress that means they may run in parallel; the reference's token loop is inherently sequential.

The two remaining lines of the block are the MLP and the residual stream:

x_residual = x
x = rmsnorm(x)
x = linear(x, state_dict[f'layer{li}.mlp_fc1'])
x = [xi.relu() for xi in x]
x = linear(x, state_dict[f'layer{li}.mlp_fc2'])
x = [a + b for a, b in zip(x, x_residual)]

mlp(x: Vec): Vec = W_out relu(W_in x) is the first formula; forward is the second, with X' as the primed intermediate. (Two small elementwise helpers at the top of the figure lift + and rmsnorm to a whole sequence; matrices() lists the layer's parameters for the optimizer.)

5.4 Embeddings, layers, logits

tok_emb = state_dict['wte'][token_id] # token embedding
pos_emb = state_dict['wpe'][pos_id] # position embedding
x = [t + p for t, p in zip(tok_emb, pos_emb)] # joint token and position embedding
x = rmsnorm(x)
for li in range(n_layer):
    ...
logits = linear(x, state_dict['lm_head'])

The token embedding table E and the position table P are matrices whose rows are looked up by subscript; the input at position t is rmsnorm(E[tokens[t]] + P[t]). Layers are applied in order (the only genuinely sequential loop in the forward pass), and W_lm x maps each final vector to one logit per vocabulary entry. params() flattens every matrix into the single parameter list the optimizer walks.

5.5 Parameters

The reference initializes each matrix with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.08 and keeps them in a dictionary; in Fortress the matrices are constructor arguments of Layer and Model, built from lists of numbers by Mat(⟨ Vec(⟨ node(x) | x ← row ⟩) | row ← rows ⟩). For the verification run the numbers are the reference's own initial weights (dumped from the seeded Python run); the demo in section 6 starts from the same weights. Fortress's library has no Gaussian generator, so a uniform-based initializer is used only in the smoke test.

matrix = lambda nout, nin, std=0.08: [[Value(random.gauss(0, std)) for _ in range(nin)] for _ in range(nout)]
state_dict = {'wte': matrix(vocab_size, n_embd), 'wpe': matrix(block_size, n_embd), 'lm_head': matrix(vocab_size, n_embd)}
for i in range(n_layer):
    state_dict[f'layer{i}.attn_wq'] = matrix(n_embd, n_embd)
    ...
params = [p for mat in state_dict.values() for row in mat for p in row]

5.6 The same attention one token at a time (the KV cache)

The reference's formulation is an incremental one: a layer object keeps the keys and values of the positions seen so far, and a call handles one new token. This is exactly the same mathematics with the sequence loop turned inside out — for the current token's query q:

The verified Fortress version of that form (src/alt/v2_kvcache_MicroGPT.fss) makes the cache two mutable lists on the layer and writes one head as alpha = softmax((K[cols] q[cols]) / SQRT(d_h)), alpha V[cols]:

Both forms produce identical logits and gradients (section 7). The stateless sequence form was chosen as primary because the model becomes a pure function of its input, positions are independent iterations, and the notation matches the papers; the cached form remains the natural one for generating text token by token, which is why the reference uses it everywhere.

6. Loss, backpropagation, Adam, training loop, sampling

6.1 Cross-entropy loss

Each training document is a name wrapped in the special BOS token on both sides. For every position the model predicts the next token; the loss is the negative log-probability it assigned to the token that actually came next, averaged over the positions:

keys, values = [[] for _ in range(n_layer)], [[] for _ in range(n_layer)]
losses = []
for pos_id in range(n):
    token_id, target_id = tokens[pos_id], tokens[pos_id + 1]
    logits = gpt(token_id, pos_id, keys, values)
    probs = softmax(logits)
    loss_t = -probs[target_id].log()
    losses.append(loss_t)
loss = (1 / n) * sum(losses) # final average loss over the document sequence. May yours be low.

The sequence form calls the model once on the first n tokens and reads one logit vector per position. The result is a single Value at the root of a graph with about 8 400 nodes per position; loss.backward() (section 2) fills the grad field of all 4 192 parameters.

6.2 Adam

Adam keeps two running averages per parameter — of the gradient and of its square — corrects their start-up bias, and steps each parameter by their ratio; microgpt also decays the learning rate linearly over training.

for i, p in enumerate(params):
    m[i] = beta1 * m[i] + (1 - beta1) * p.grad
    v[i] = beta2 * v[i] + (1 - beta2) * p.grad ** 2
    m_hat = m[i] / (1 - beta1 ** (step + 1))
    v_hat = v[i] / (1 - beta2 ** (step + 1))
    p.data -= lr_t * m_hat / (v_hat ** 0.5 + eps_adam)
    p.grad = 0

This is the one place where Fortify's typesetting adds notation on its own: beta1 becomes β1, m_hat becomes m̂, and the update reads as the formula. The buffers m, v are plain arrays of numbers indexed like the parameter list, and the step count t lives in the optimizer object rather than in the training loop.

6.3 The training loop

The reference trains for 1 000 steps, one document per step. The Fortress demo is bounded: it starts from the reference's initial weights, takes 12 steps over the first documents of the seeded, shuffled dataset, and then samples. Tokenization is the character index in the sorted alphabet with BOS added at both ends:

doc = docs[step % len(docs)]
tokens = [BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [BOS]
n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)
# ... forward, loss, loss.backward(), Adam update ...
lr_t = learning_rate * (1 - step / num_steps) # linear learning rate decay

Output of the demo run. Its first two losses are the reference's own steps 1 and 2 (3.3660 and 3.4243 in the microgpt article), because both start from the same weights and the same documents; after twelve steps the loss has moved from about 3.37 (near ln 27 = 3.30, uniform guessing) to about 3.0, and the sampled strings are not yet name-like — the reference needs its full thousand steps for that, which at 35 s per step is outside this experiment's bounded runs.

6.4 Sampling

Generation feeds the model its own output: start from BOS, turn the logits at the last position into probabilities (divided by a temperature that sharpens the distribution), draw a token, append it, repeat until BOS or the block size. The draw picks the first index whose cumulative probability exceeds a uniform number — the rule random.choices implements.

for pos_id in range(block_size):
    logits = gpt(token_id, pos_id, keys, values)
    probs = softmax([l / temperature for l in logits])
    token_id = random.choices(range(vocab_size), weights=[p.data for p in probs])[0]
    if token_id == BOS:
        break
    sample.append(uchars[token_id])

In the sequence form the model is re-run on the growing prefix at every step (quadratic in the length, but the block size is 16); the cached form of section 5.6 is the linear-time way to do the same. The verification run replays the uniform draws recorded from the Python sampler, so the two programs pick identical tokens.

7. Verification against the reference, and cost

Reference. Karpathy's microgpt.py gist (8627fe009c40f57531cb18360106ce95), revision 14fb038816c7aae0bb9342c2dbf1a51dd134a5ff, 199 lines, sha256 d47d88c2fd432c8ebdc1048beab7f7eb64ea7e0e664e11b812d72a6d95ebccee, with the names dataset it pins (makemore names.txt at commit 988aa59, 32 032 names). The article and the gist agree on all model, autograd, optimizer and inference code; the gist additionally seeds the random generator (42), which the checks rely on.

Check data. A harness (tools/derive_checks.py) executes the pinned source verbatim up to the optimizer section — seed, data shuffle, tokenizer, Value, parameter initialization, model — and then runs an arithmetically identical, instrumented copy of the training loop for two steps and of the inference loop for three samples, recording: the initial weights; per position the logits, probabilities and loss; the total loss; every gradient; the Adam-updated parameters; and, for sampling, the per-step probabilities, the uniform draws consumed by random.choices and the chosen tokens. Its two losses, 3.365967 and 3.424273, are the values printed in the microgpt article for steps 1 and 2. The data is exported as a generated Fortress component (src/MicroGPTData.fss, decimal literals that round-trip exactly).

Checks. The check program builds the model from the reference's initial weights and, for each step, compares 27 logits at every position, the per-position losses and the loss, then runs backward and Adam and compares all 4 192 gradients and updated parameters matrix by matrix; then it samples three names replaying the recorded draws and compares probabilities, tokens and text. Tolerance: 10-12 absolute, four orders of magnitude above the largest observed difference and four below the smallest quantity of interest (gradients are O(10-3–10-1), Adam updates O(10-2)). The only source of difference is summation order: Python's sum is a left fold, a Fortress ∑ combines terms in the order its generator chooses, which perturbs a 16–64-term dot product at the 10-16 level.

The interpreter (the 2012 Java tree-walker, single-threaded here) is three orders of magnitude slower than CPython on this workload. None of the notation above was chosen for speed; the sequence form happens to be the fastest of the three because the per-position comprehension avoids the cache bookkeeping.

8. What the language gives, what we added, where the mismatches remain

Given by Fortress

  • Operators as library code. +, juxtaposition, ^, DOT, || are ordinary operator declarations (opr), so a user type takes part in arithmetic notation with the same precedence and typesetting as numbers. Juxtaposition being multiplication is what makes W x, alpha V, scale x and n data^(n-1) read as formulas.
  • Generators, reductions, comprehensions. Every collection is a generator; SUM[i <- g] e, BIG MAX, BIG || and ⟨ e | x ← g ⟩ desugar into a generator's generate with a reduction object; the same desugaring makes iterations implicitly parallel. Adding a big operator for a new type is a seven-line reduction object plus a two-line operator.
  • Traits with default behavior. DelegatedIndexed gives Vec the whole generator protocol from a handful of delegations; CommutativeMonoidReduction and MonoidReduction supply the reduction plumbing.
  • Static sizes and nat arithmetic exist (Array1⟦T,0,n⟧, d+d) and were used in the first design.
  • Fortify. Subscripts, Greek letters, hats, blackboard types, the big operators with their bindings, fractions for 1/data, and √ are all produced from the ASCII source.

Added at user level (all shown in the figures above)

  • the autograd Value with 13 operator/method definitions, the node factory, three mixed-operand operators, topo, the id counter;
  • SumValues + the two ∑ operators, after hiding the library's ∑ with an except import;
  • Vec (six delegations, six operators), CatVecs + BIG ||, Mat (four subscripts, entries, two juxtapositions), relu on vectors, and two sequence-lifting helpers.

Line counts of the primary program (non-blank, non-comment): mathematical core — Value operations 27, Vec 20, Mat 9, rmsnorm 5, softmax 6, layer 25, model 9, loss 6, Adam 16, sampler 12; supporting machinery — topological sort 12, ∑ 7, ids/imports/headers 21; smoke test 27. Total 202 lines against the reference's 199 lines of Python, which fold the tokenizer, the training loop and inference into the same file (in Fortress those live in the generated data component and the demo driver).

Items that would make the historical system better at this task without changing its design — a revival worklist: (1) a ∑ defined over an additive-monoid trait instead of the sealed Number; (2) unification of T[n]/T^n types with runtime arrays of any element type; (3) the subscript-then-subscript/superscript evaluation bug; (4) API-boundary instantiation of nat-generic functions; (5) inferring the element type of list literals from context; (6) Fortify's handling of subscripted identifiers followed by an index.

9. Alternatives explored, and why this form

Three complete, verified programs were written before choosing; each passes the same 52 checks against the reference. They differ in how vectors are typed, how the matrix–vector product is written, and whether the model carries state.

v1 — arrays and indicesv2 — Vec/Mat, one token at a timev3 — Vec/Mat, whole sequence (primary)
vector typeIndexed⟦Value,ℤ32⟧ parameters, List resultsVecVec
weightsArray2⟦Value,0,m,0,n⟧ with nat parametersMat (rows)Mat (rows)
W x⟨ ∑j←0#n Wi,j xj | i ← 0#m ⟩⟨ w·x | w ← W.rows ⟩same
attentionper component, ⟨ ∑t αt (vt)j | j ⟩softmax((Kcols qcols)/√dh), α Vcolssoftmax((Kh0:t Qht)/√dh), α Vh0:t
stateKV cacheKV cachenone; positions are a comprehension
sourcesrc/alt/v1_MicroGPT.fsssrc/alt/v2_kvcache_MicroGPT.fsssrc/MicroGPT.fss

The array design (v1) is closest to Fortress's own library idiom — sizes in types, indices under the ∑ — and its formulas typeset well, but the interpreter does not accept the abbreviated Value[n] types, so every signature spells Indexed⟦Value,ℤ32⟧ or Array2⟦Value,0,m,0,n⟧, and its attention had to be written per component because a sliced array is no longer a sized array. Its layer:

Moving to Vec/Mat (v2) is what made softmax(K q/√d) V expressible. Turning the token loop into a sequence function (v3) removed the mutable cache and made positions independent iterations; it also shortened the loss to a single call. The remaining visible seams in v3 are: Mat(⟨ W_q x | x ← X ⟩) where a paper writes XWq⊤ (a matrix–matrix product was not needed anywhere else, so none was defined); .cols(c) for head selection; the parenthesized (headsh)[t] forced by the interpreter bug; and the BIG ‖ spelling of head concatenation.

Autograd representations

Pairs (chosen), parallel lists (Python's shape) and closures (micrograd's original) are compared in section 2; all three run. The pairs form is the only one whose operator definitions carry no static-argument annotations.

One ∑ for scalars and vectors

A single reduction over an Additive trait with an explicit Zero lets the same ∑ sum Values and Vecs, so the head output could be written ∑t αt vt instead of alpha V. It runs correctly (the interpreter checks types at run time), but the static result type is Additive; the specification's overloading rules leave no way to give the nullary ∑ a result type that depends on the body. This is the one place where a genuinely nicer notation was declined for typing honesty.

What “canonical” means here

The chosen form is canonical in the sense that every operation of the model is written with the operator or big operator the mathematics uses, on types that name the mathematical object (Value, Vec, Mat), with no annotations in the model's definitions, and that the same definitions execute and reproduce the reference bit-for-bit up to summation order. It is not unique: the array form is equally correct and arguably more idiomatic for Fortress's numeric library; it was set aside because of interpreter gaps, not because of the language.

10. Reproducing everything

All files live under experiment/worker/ of the repository; the interpreter is the historical Fortress tree, unmodified.

source experiment/env.sh                                   # Java 25, single-thread interpreter
experiment/worker/run.sh experiment/worker/src/MicroGPT.fss # smoke test with random weights (~35 s)
python3 experiment/worker/tools/derive_checks.py 2 3         # needs reference/microgpt.py + input.txt (not committed)
python3 experiment/worker/tools/gen_data.py                  # -> src/MicroGPTData.{fsi,fss} (committed)
python3 experiment/worker/tools/build.py                     # -> build/Check.fss
cp experiment/worker/src/MicroGPTData.* experiment/worker/build/
experiment/worker/run.sh experiment/worker/build/Check.fss  # 52 checks, ~2 min
python3 experiment/worker/tools/build.py experiment/worker/src/MicroGPT.fss train_main.part Train
experiment/worker/run.sh experiment/worker/build/Train.fss  # bounded training demo, ~15 min
python3 experiment/worker/tools/figs.py experiment/worker/src/MicroGPT.fss gpt   # typeset the figures
python3 experiment/worker/tools/build_article.py            # this page
  • notes/01-orientation.md — the checkout survey and every probe's finding with evidence; notes/02-v1-verified.md, notes/03-design.md, notes/gaps.md — milestone notes (attempt, observation, decision, uncertainty) and the classified gap list.
  • probes/ — 39 small runnable programs, failures included; transcript.txt — every interpreter and typesetting invocation with its output.
  • checks/checks_2steps.json — the reference-derived data; checks/check_run_v{1,2,3}_output.txt, checks/train_demo_output.txt — run outputs.
  • figures/*.tic, *.svg — figure sources and renderings; article/sections/*.html and article/math_table.py — this article's sources.

The reference Python and dataset are not committed (their licenses are unstated); they are fetched from the pinned URLs by the commands in notes/01-orientation.md. Fortress and Fortify are Sun Microsystems / Oracle work under their own license in the repository root.
